questions.title: Essential JVM Flags — -Xms, -Xmx, -XX Categories, and How to Inspect Them
questions.question: What are the essential JVM heap-sizing flags? Explain the -XX flag categories and how to inspect a running JVM's effective values.
questions.direct_answer: The essential heap flags are `-Xms` (initial heap size), `-Xmx` (max heap size), `-Xss` (per-thread stack size), and `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` (Metaspace cap). For containers, prefer `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` over hardcoded `-Xmx`. The `-XX` flags fall into three categories: **product** (always available), **diagnostic** (require `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions`), and **experimental** (require `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions`). Inspect a running JVM's effective flag values with `jcmd <pid> VM.flags`, `jinfo -flags <pid>`, or by adding `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` at startup. Best practice: set `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` to avoid heap resizing pauses, never set `-Xmx` to the full container memory limit, and always pair production flags with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the flags that actually matter in production and can inspect live JVM configuration to debug
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting -Xms much smaller than -Xmx (causes long pauses as heap resizes during the first hour of life) or setting -Xmx equal to container memory limit (triggers OOMKill from non-heap memory)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish product/diagnostic/experimental flag categories, mention `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` for discovering all defaults, and explain why `-Xms == -Xmx` is the production norm

sections.title: JVM Flags Are an Operational Vocabulary, Not a Tuning Cookbook
sections.content:
Most production Java tuning involves under a dozen flags — but knowing **which** dozen, and how to inspect their effective values on a running JVM, separates someone who can debug a production incident at 3am from someone who copy-pastes flags from a blog post and hopes for the best. The JVM exposes hundreds of flags; you do not need to memorize them, but you do need to know the categories and how to look them up.

Flags fall into three categories distinguished by their command-line prefix and unlock requirements:

- **Standard options** start with `-X` (e.g., `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-Xss`). These are the heap and stack sizing flags every JVM supports. They are stable across JVM versions and well-documented.
- **Non-standard options** start with `-XX:` and divide into three subcategories: **product** flags (always available, e.g., `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`), **diagnostic** flags (require `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions` to enable, used for debugging), and **experimental** flags (require `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions`, may change between releases).
- **Boolean toggle syntax** — `-XX:+FlagName` enables a feature, `-XX:-FlagName` disables it. Numeric flags use `=`, e.g., `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`.

The operational discipline: in production you set the small set of flags that actually matter (heap, GC choice, GC logging, OOM diagnostics), inspect the effective values on running JVMs to confirm what's actually applied, and use diagnostic/experimental flags only with explicit purpose.

sections.title: The Essential Production Flags — What Each Does
sections.content:
These are the flags worth memorizing. Every other flag is something you look up when you need it.

| Flag | Purpose | Production Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-Xms<size>` | Initial heap size | Set equal to `-Xmx` |
| `-Xmx<size>` | Maximum heap size | Set explicitly; in containers prefer `MaxRAMPercentage` |
| `-Xss<size>` | Per-thread stack size | 512KB-1MB; reduce only if many threads |
| `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=<size>` | Cap Metaspace growth | 256MB-512MB depending on app |
| `-XX:+UseG1GC` | Choose G1 collector | Default since Java 9 |
| `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` | G1 soft pause-time target | 200ms default |
| `-XX:+UseZGC` | Choose ZGC for low latency | When p99 < 10ms required |
| `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` | Container-aware heap sizing | 75% leaves room for non-heap |
| `-Xlog:gc*:file=...` | GC logging (Java 9+) | Always enable |
| `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` | Auto heap dump on OOM | Always enable |
| `-XX:HeapDumpPath=<dir>` | Where to write OOM dumps | Persistent volume in containers |
| `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` | Hard exit on OOM | Recommended in containers |

**Why `-Xms == -Xmx` in production.** When `-Xms` is much smaller than `-Xmx`, the JVM grows the heap incrementally as the application's working set expands. Each growth is a stop-the-world event that can take seconds on large heaps. Setting them equal pre-allocates the full heap at startup so the OS commits the memory once and the JVM never resizes. This trades startup memory for predictable steady-state behavior — exactly the right trade-off for long-running services.

**Why never `-Xmx == container memory limit`.** A 1GB container with `-Xmx=1g` will be OOM-killed by the kernel even if the heap never exceeds 1GB. The heap is only one part of JVM memory — Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, and direct buffers easily add 300-500MB on top. Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` (or 70 for Netty-heavy apps) so the JVM leaves room for non-heap memory.

sections.title: Inspecting a Running JVM's Effective Flags
sections.content:
Knowing how to inspect a running JVM is half the operational skill. There are three common methods.

**Method 1: `jcmd VM.flags` (preferred, on a running process).**

```bash
# All set flags (only those overridden from defaults)
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

# All flags including defaults
jcmd <pid> VM.flags -all
```

Output shows every flag the JVM is actually using, including those set on the command line and those set internally by ergonomics (the JVM's auto-tuning logic). This is the ground truth — not what was passed on the command line, but what the JVM actually has in effect.

**Method 2: `jinfo -flags` (compatible alternative).**

```bash
jinfo -flags <pid>
```

**Method 3: `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` at startup (discovery).**

```bash
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | less
```

This dumps every flag the JVM knows about with its current value, type, and whether it was set on the command line, set by ergonomics, or kept at the default. It is the canonical reference for "what flags exist on this JVM version?" Use it to discover flags you might want to tune.

**A typical line:**

```
     uintx MaxHeapSize                            = 4294967296                                {product} {ergonomic}
```

Decoded:
- `uintx` — type (unsigned integer)
- `MaxHeapSize` — internal name (corresponds to `-Xmx`)
- `= 4294967296` — current value (4GB)
- `{product}` — flag category (always available)
- `{ergonomic}` — value source (set by JVM auto-tuning, not by command line)

The `{ergonomic}` annotation is important — it tells you the JVM auto-derived this value rather than you setting it. If you expected `-Xmx=8g` and see `4294967296` ergonomic, your flag wasn't applied (perhaps consumed by a wrapper script).

**Method 4: `jcmd VM.system_properties`** for `-D` system properties, and `jcmd VM.command_line` for the actual command line that started the JVM.

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
# VM Arguments:
# jvm_args: -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+UseG1GC ...
# java_command: com.example.MyApp
```

In production debugging, the workflow is: start with `jcmd VM.command_line` to see what was passed, then `jcmd VM.flags` to see what's actually applied — discrepancies often explain weird behavior.

sections.title: Choosing Heap and Stack Sizes — Practical Heuristics
sections.content:
Choosing heap size is part workload analysis and part trial and error. Here are the heuristics that work in practice.

**Sizing the heap (`-Xmx`):**
- Run with a generous initial guess (e.g., 4GB) and capture GC logs over a representative load period
- Look at post-full-GC live set in GCEasy — that's your baseline working set
- Set `-Xmx` to roughly **2-3× the post-full-GC live set** for healthy minor GC margins
- Too small: frequent full GCs and high CPU overhead
- Too large: longer GC pauses (especially for non-G1 collectors) and wasted container memory

**Setting `-Xms`:**
- In production, **always set equal to `-Xmx`** — avoids heap-resize pauses
- In dev/local, you can set smaller (e.g., 256MB) to keep memory footprint low

**Sizing thread stacks (`-Xss`):**
- Default is 1MB on most platforms — fine for most apps
- Reduce to 512KB or 256KB when running thousands of threads (e.g., legacy thread-per-request servers)
- Increase only if you're getting `StackOverflowError` from deep recursion (better fix: refactor the recursion)
- For virtual threads (Java 21+): `-Xss` does not apply; virtual thread stacks are dynamically sized

**Sizing Metaspace (`-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`):**
- Default is unlimited — dangerous in containers (can fill all available memory)
- Always set explicitly: 256MB for typical Spring Boot, 512MB for very large apps with many classes
- Hot-redeploy environments (Tomcat with multiple WARs) need higher caps and require monitoring for ClassLoader leaks

**Container-aware heap (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`):**
- 75% is a reasonable default for most services
- 70% for Netty/Spring WebFlux services that use significant direct buffer memory
- 60% for services that load large native libraries (e.g., TensorFlow Java bindings)
- Always pair with explicit Kubernetes `resources.limits.memory`

**Anti-patterns to avoid:**
- Setting `-Xss` to 16MB "just to be safe" — multiplies thread memory cost by 16x
- Hardcoding `-Xmx2g` in a pod spec without setting matching memory limits
- Tuning heap size based on "how much RAM does the host have" instead of measured working set
- Copying flag combinations from old blog posts that target deprecated collectors

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Standard `-X` flags** — `-Xms`, `-Xmx`, `-Xss`; the heap and stack sizing essentials.
- **`-XX:` flags have three categories** — product (always available), diagnostic (need `UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions`), experimental (need `UnlockExperimentalVMOptions`).
- **Boolean toggle syntax** — `-XX:+Flag` enables, `-XX:-Flag` disables; numeric uses `=`.
- **Set `-Xms == -Xmx`** in production — avoids heap-resize pauses.
- **Never set `-Xmx` to container memory limit** — non-heap memory will trigger OOMKill; use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`.
- **Cap Metaspace explicitly** — `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m`; default is unlimited.
- **Inspect live JVM** with `jcmd VM.flags` (effective), `VM.command_line` (what was passed), `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` (all available).
- **Always enable in production** — `-Xlog:gc*`, `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`, `-XX:HeapDumpPath`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JVM flags can feel overwhelming because there are hundreds of them, but the production-essential set is small — under a dozen flags handle 95% of real-world tuning needs.

**The essential flags:**
- `-Xms` and `-Xmx` — initial and max heap; **always set them equal in production** to avoid heap-resize pauses
- `-Xss` — per-thread stack size; default 512KB-1MB; usually leave alone
- `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` — cap Metaspace; **always set explicitly** since the default is unlimited
- `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` — for containers; uses 75% of cgroup memory limit as max heap
- `-XX:+UseG1GC` — default since Java 9; usually no need to change
- `-Xlog:gc*` — GC logging; always enable in production
- `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` — auto-dump on OOM; always enable

**Three flag categories distinguished by `-XX` prefix:**
- **Product** — always available, e.g., `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`
- **Diagnostic** — requires `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions` to enable
- **Experimental** — requires `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions`

**Inspecting a running JVM's effective flags:**
- `jcmd <pid> VM.flags` — what's actually in effect (preferred)
- `jcmd <pid> VM.command_line` — what was passed on the command line
- `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` at startup — discover all available flags and defaults

**Two production anti-patterns to avoid:**
1. **`-Xms` much smaller than `-Xmx`** — causes long heap-resize pauses in the first hour of life
2. **`-Xmx` equal to container memory limit** — non-heap memory (Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers) easily adds 300-500MB; the kernel OOMKills before the heap ever hits its max

In an interview, the differentiator is mentioning `jcmd VM.flags` for inspecting the live state — most candidates know about `-Xmx` but few can debug a JVM whose actual configuration doesn't match what they think they passed.

questions.question: How do you optimize JVM startup time? What are Virtual Threads (Project Loom)?
questions.title: JVM Startup Optimization and Virtual Threads (Java 21)
questions.direct_answer: Reduce JVM startup with CDS (Class Data Sharing), AppCDS, or GraalVM native image. Virtual Threads (Java 21) are lightweight JVM-managed threads mapped to OS threads dynamically, eliminating thread pool sizing constraints for I/O-bound services.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern JVM features important for cloud/serverless and high-concurrency services
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking virtual threads eliminate the need for async/reactive programming entirely — CPU-bound tasks still need reactive approaches
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that virtual threads are parked (not pinned) during I/O, and explain thread pinning as the current limitation

sections.title: Spring Boot Takes 3-10 Seconds to Start Because It Classloads and Reflects — CDS and Virtual Threads Attack Different Bottlenecks
sections.content:
JVM startup time and concurrent I/O throughput are two separate problems that get conflated in interviews. **Startup optimization** targets the 3-10 seconds a typical Spring Boot application spends loading classes, scanning annotations, and creating beans. **Virtual Threads** target the thread-per-request scalability ceiling where a 200-thread pool limits you to 200 concurrent I/O operations.

For startup, the bottleneck is **class loading and verification**. The JVM reads thousands of `.class` files from JARs, parses bytecode, verifies type safety, and builds internal metadata structures. **AppCDS** (Application Class Data Sharing) pre-processes these classes into a shared archive that the JVM memory-maps at startup, cutting classloading time by 20-40%. Spring Boot's **AOT processing** takes a different angle — it generates bean definitions as source code at build time, eliminating the reflection-based classpath scanning that dominates startup.

Virtual Threads solve a fundamentally different problem. Traditional platform threads map 1:1 to OS threads — each costs ~1MB of stack memory and an OS scheduling entity. Virtual threads are JVM-managed, weighing only a few hundred bytes. When a virtual thread calls blocking I/O, it **parks** (unmounts from its carrier OS thread) rather than blocking the carrier.

This means existing synchronous code — JDBC calls, `RestTemplate`, file I/O — becomes I/O-concurrent without rewriting as reactive. The critical limitation is **thread pinning**: `synchronized` blocks and JNI calls pin the virtual thread to its carrier, defeating the scheduling advantage.

sections.title: AppCDS Archives, Virtual Thread Scheduling, and the Pinning Trap
sections.content:
Setting up **AppCDS** requires three steps: generate a class list by running the application once, create a shared archive from that list, and launch with the archive. The archive is a memory-mapped file that skips parsing and verification for pre-processed classes.

```bash
# Step 1: Record which classes the app loads
java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=classes.lst -jar app.jar

# Step 2: Build the shared archive from the class list
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=classes.lst \
     -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -jar app.jar

# Step 3: Launch with the archive (20-40% faster startup)
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -jar app.jar
```

The archive must be regenerated when dependencies change, so CI pipelines typically rebuild it alongside the application JAR.

Virtual Threads become available through `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or Spring Boot 3.2's `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`. The JVM schedules virtual threads onto a small pool of **carrier threads** (defaulting to the number of CPU cores). When a virtual thread hits a blocking call, the JVM unmounts it from the carrier and mounts another ready virtual thread — this is why millions of virtual threads can run on a handful of OS threads.

The **pinning trap** is the production issue most teams encounter first. When code executes inside a `synchronized` block during a blocking call, the virtual thread cannot unmount — it pins the carrier thread, reducing the effective carrier pool. Detect pinning with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` and replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` on I/O paths. **ThreadLocal** abuse is the second trap — each virtual thread maintains its own copy, so a `ThreadLocal<byte[]>` with a 64KB buffer across a million virtual threads consumes 64GB of heap. Audit all ThreadLocals and migrate to `ScopedValue` where possible.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **AppCDS** — capture loaded classes once; build shared archive; subsequent launches memory-map instead of re-parsing; 20-40% faster startup.
- **Spring Boot AOT** — generates bean definitions at build time; eliminates runtime reflection scanning.
- **GraalVM native image** — sub-200ms startup; demands explicit reflection configuration for all dynamic access.
- **Virtual threads: ~1KB stack, JVM-scheduled** — blocking I/O unmounts the carrier; existing synchronous code scales.
- **Pinning: `synchronized` blocks prevent unmounting** — replace with `ReentrantLock` on I/O paths; detect with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Modern JVM performance optimization addresses two distinct goals: faster startup time (targeted by AOT compilation, AppCDS, and Spring AOT) and higher concurrency without scaling thread counts (addressed by virtual threads in Java 21+). These are separate problems solved by separate mechanisms.

**Startup optimization options:**
- AppCDS: capture loaded classes once, build a shared archive, subsequent launches memory-map instead of re-parsing; cuts startup 20-40%
- Spring Boot AOT: generates bean definitions at build time, eliminating runtime reflection scanning
- GraalVM native image: sub-200ms startup; demands explicit reflection configuration for all dynamic access

**Virtual threads (Java 21):**
- JVM-managed lightweight threads mounting onto a small pool of carrier threads (~N cores)
- Blocking I/O parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier — existing synchronous code scales to thousands of concurrent I/O operations
- No reactive rewriting needed — keep your blocking JDBC calls and HTTP clients

**Thread pinning (main migration concern):**
- `synchronized` block pins the virtual thread to its carrier — cannot unmount; if the block contains I/O, the carrier is wasted
- Fix: replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` on I/O-heavy paths
- Enable `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` during testing to detect pinning before production

I recommend AOT for startup-sensitive deployments and virtual threads for I/O-heavy services. Audit all `ThreadLocal` usage — each virtual thread maintains its own copy, which can waste memory at scale.

questions.question: How should you configure JVM settings for a Spring Boot application running in a container?
questions.title: JVM Settings for Spring Boot in Docker/Kubernetes
questions.direct_answer: Use container-aware JVM flags: -XX:+UseContainerSupport (Java 8u191+, default in Java 11+) lets JVM read cgroup limits. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 to leave OS overhead. Avoid hardcoded -Xmx — it ignores container memory limits and causes OOMKilled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical containerization knowledge for Java services
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting -Xmx to the container memory limit (e.g., -Xmx512m for a 512m container) — no room for metaspace, direct buffers, or OS overhead → OOMKilled
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that non-heap memory (metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers) is significant and must be accounted for

sections.title: Without Container-Aware Flags, Your JVM Sees 64 Cores and 256GB RAM on a Shared Node
sections.content:
Java applications in containers face a fundamental mismatch: the JVM's default behavior reads the **host's** CPU count and total memory, not the container's cgroup limits. A pod limited to 2 CPUs and 1GB of memory can start a JVM that detects 64 CPUs and 256GB RAM, creating 64 GC threads, oversizing the `ForkJoinPool`, and allocating a heap that exceeds the container's memory budget. The result is `OOMKilled` — the Linux kernel terminates the process because it exceeded the cgroup memory limit.

**`-XX:+UseContainerSupport`** (default since Java 11) tells the JVM to read cgroup v1/v2 limits. The critical companion flag is **`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`**, which sets the maximum heap to 75% of the container's memory limit. The remaining 25% covers **non-heap memory**: Metaspace (class metadata, 100-150MB typical), code cache (JIT-compiled code, 50-100MB), thread stacks (each thread consumes the `-Xss` value, default 512KB-1MB), direct byte buffers (Netty, NIO), and OS overhead.

The most common production mistake is setting **`-Xmx` equal to the container memory limit** — for example, `-Xmx512m` for a 512MB container. This leaves zero room for non-heap memory, and the process gets `OOMKilled` even though the heap never exceeded its limit. The rule of thumb is that total JVM memory consumption equals **heap × 1.5 minimum** — so a 512MB heap needs at least 768MB of container memory. For Kubernetes, always set both `resources.requests.memory` (determines scheduling) and `resources.limits.memory` (triggers OOMKill if exceeded), with the limit generously covering non-heap overhead.

sections.title: Memory Budget Breakdown and Kubernetes Deployment Configuration
sections.content:
Understanding exactly where memory goes inside a JVM container prevents the most common `OOMKilled` scenarios. For a container with a 1GB memory limit and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`, the budget breaks down as follows.

| Memory Area | Typical Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Heap (MaxRAMPercentage=75%) | ~750MB | GC-managed object storage |
| Metaspace | 100-150MB | Class metadata, grows with loaded classes |
| Code Cache | 50-100MB | JIT-compiled native code |
| Thread Stacks (100 threads x 512KB) | ~50MB | Configurable with -Xss |
| Direct Buffers | Varies | Netty, NIO off-heap allocations |
| OS/Kernel overhead | ~50MB | Page tables, mapped files |
| **Total** | ~1050-1150MB | Exceeds 1GB limit |

This budget shows why 75% is already aggressive for heap — the non-heap components easily consume 300-400MB. For **Netty-heavy** services (Spring WebFlux, gRPC), direct buffer usage can add another 100-200MB, requiring a larger container or a lower `MaxRAMPercentage`.

The Kubernetes pod specification should set both requests and limits, with JVM flags passed through an environment variable that the entrypoint script consumes.

```yaml
containers:
- name: order-service
  image: myapp:1.0
  env:
  - name: JAVA_OPTS
    value: >-
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
      -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
      -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/
      -Xss512k
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: "768Mi"    # scheduler places pod on adequate node
      cpu: "500m"
    limits:
      memory: "1Gi"      # kernel OOMKills if exceeded
      cpu: "2"
```

Setting `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` is essential for container diagnostics — when the JVM hits heap exhaustion, it writes a heap dump before the container restarts. Mount a persistent volume at `/dumps/` so the dump survives the pod restart. For CPU, limiting to 2 cores prevents one JVM from starving neighbor pods on the same node and ensures the JVM correctly sizes its internal thread pools based on the available processors rather than total host cores.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Without container awareness, JVM sees host resources** — sizes heap and thread pools for the node, not the container.
- **Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`** — not hardcoded `-Xmx`; leaves 25% for Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers.
- **Rule of thumb: container memory >= heap x 1.5** — `-Xmx` matching container limit triggers OOMKill from non-heap usage.
- **Set both `requests` and `limits` in Kubernetes** — requests for scheduling; limits trigger OOMKill when exceeded.
- **`UseContainerSupport` is on by default since Java 10** — JVM reads cgroup limits; CPU limits ensure correct pool sizing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Running the JVM inside a container requires explicit resource configuration — without it, the JVM reads the host machine's total memory and CPU count and sizes the heap and thread pools for the full node, often blowing past the container's actual memory limit and triggering an OOMKill.

**MaxRAMPercentage over -Xmx:**
- `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` instead of hardcoded `-Xmx` — uses 75% of container's memory limit as max heap
- Leaves 25% for non-heap: Metaspace (100-150MB), code cache (50-100MB), thread stacks (512KB each), direct buffers
- `-Xmx` matching the container limit → total JVM memory exceeds the limit → Linux OOMKill

**Kubernetes resource settings:**
- Set both `resources.requests.memory` and `resources.limits.memory`
- Requests: determines which node the pod lands on (scheduling)
- Limits: triggers OOMKill when exceeded
- Rule of thumb: container memory ≥ heap × 1.5

**CPU limits:**
- Set CPU limits to prevent one JVM from consuming all node CPU
- Ensures JVM correctly sizes GC threads and ForkJoinPool based on available processors, not total host cores
- `UseContainerSupport` is enabled by default since Java 10 — reads cgroup limits automatically

I recommend enabling `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and mounting a persistent volume for heap dumps — you don't want to lose diagnostic evidence when a container restarts after OOMKill.

questions.title: Tuning the JVM for Microservices in Containers — CPU Quotas, Memory Pressure, and Cold Starts
questions.question: How do you tune a JVM running as a microservice in containers? Explain how CPU quotas, container memory limits, and JVM ergonomics interact.
questions.direct_answer: JVMs in containers face three problems traditional tuning ignores: **CPU quotas** that throttle threads even when CPU count is correct, **memory limits** that the JVM must read from cgroups (not the host), and **cold start latency** that matters because containers come and go. Tune with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70-75` (leaves room for non-heap), `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount` if cgroup detection is unreliable, **AppCDS** or **CRaC** to cut startup time by 50-90%, and **G1** for general workloads or **ZGC** for latency-critical services with heaps over 4GB. Always set Kubernetes `requests` ≈ `limits` for memory (avoids overcommit), use **CPU requests with no limits** to avoid throttling, and pair production flags with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` writing to a persistent volume.

sections.title: Containers Change Three Things About JVM Tuning
sections.content:
Tuning a JVM for a long-running bare-metal server is a stable problem with well-known answers. Tuning a JVM for a microservice running in a container — usually Kubernetes — is a different problem with different failure modes. Three things change.

**First, the JVM has to discover its own resources from cgroups.** On a bare-metal server, `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()` returns the host's CPU count and `MaxRAM` defaults to a fraction of host RAM. In a container, the JVM must read **cgroup v1 or v2 limits** to know its actual budget. Java 10+ has `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` enabled by default, but cgroup v2 (Kubernetes 1.25+) introduced subtle differences in how CPU quota is reported, and edge cases still exist where the JVM oversizes its heap or thread pools relative to what the container actually has.

**Second, CPU quotas behave differently from CPU counts.** A pod with `cpu: "2"` request and no limit gets two cores' worth of CPU on average, with bursting available. A pod with `cpu: "2"` request **and** `cpu: "2"` limit gets exactly two cores per 100ms scheduling period — and is **throttled** by the kernel for the rest of the period if it exceeds the quota. The throttling shows up as multi-millisecond pauses that are invisible to the JVM and look like mysterious latency spikes. **Garbage collection is especially sensitive** because it briefly spins up many GC threads; with CPU limits, those threads get throttled, extending GC pauses.

**Third, cold starts matter.** Containers come and go — autoscaling, rolling updates, pod evictions — and a JVM that takes 8 seconds to start is unusable in serverless environments and adds latency to deploys. **AppCDS** cuts startup by 20-40%, **Spring Boot AOT** eliminates reflection scanning, and **CRaC (Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint)** can restore a fully-warm JVM in under a second by snapshotting the running process. **GraalVM native image** gives you sub-100ms startup at the cost of build complexity and reflection limitations.

The operational discipline is to address each of these explicitly. Container-aware flags handle the first; carefully chosen Kubernetes resource specs handle the second; AppCDS, AOT, or CRaC handle the third.

sections.title: Container-Aware JVM Flag Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
These are the flags that actually matter for containerized JVMs in 2026.

| Flag | Purpose | Recommended Value |
|---|---|---|
| `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` | Read cgroup limits | Default since Java 10 |
| `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=<n>` | Heap as % of cgroup memory | 70-75 (60 for Netty) |
| `-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=<n>` | Initial heap as % | Match `MaxRAMPercentage` |
| `-XX:MinRAMPercentage=<n>` | Min heap for tiny containers | 50 (only for <256MB) |
| `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=<n>` | Override CPU detection | Set if cgroup CPU is unreliable |
| `-XX:+UseG1GC` | G1 garbage collector | Default; good for general |
| `-XX:+UseZGC` | ZGC for low latency | When p99 < 10ms required |
| `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=<size>` | Cap Metaspace | 256-512MB |
| `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` | Hard exit on OOM | Recommended in containers |
| `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` | Auto heap dump | Always enable |
| `-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/` | Where to write dumps | Persistent volume |
| `-Xlog:gc*:file=...` | GC logging (Java 9+) | Always enable |
| `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` | NMT for native memory | Enable in dev for sizing |

**Why `MaxRAMPercentage` over `-Xmx`.** A container memory budget breaks down roughly as: heap + Metaspace (~150MB) + code cache (~100MB) + thread stacks (~50MB for 100 threads) + direct buffers (variable, can be 200MB+ for Netty) + OS overhead (~50MB). For a 1GB container, that's ~350-500MB of non-heap, leaving 500-650MB for the heap. Setting `-Xmx=512m` or `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50` covers this on a 1GB container; `MaxRAMPercentage=75` works on 2GB+ containers where the absolute non-heap overhead becomes a smaller fraction.

**Why `InitialRAMPercentage == MaxRAMPercentage`.** Same reason as `-Xms == -Xmx` on bare metal: avoid heap-resize pauses. The JVM commits the full heap at startup, the OS commits the memory once, and steady-state behavior is predictable.

sections.title: CPU Quota and Throttling — The Subtle Trap
sections.content:
The most under-appreciated production issue with JVMs in Kubernetes is **CPU throttling**. It manifests as occasional latency spikes that look like GC pauses but aren't — they're the kernel pausing the entire process because it exceeded its CPU quota for the current scheduling period.

**How CPU limits work in cgroups.** The kernel allocates CPU in **CFS scheduling periods** (default 100ms). A pod with `cpu: "2"` limit gets `2 × 100ms = 200ms` of CPU time per period. If the pod uses 200ms in the first 50ms (because GC is running with multiple worker threads), it gets **throttled for the remaining 50ms** of the period — frozen by the kernel. The latency impact is invisible to the JVM (no GC pause, no lock contention) and shows up only in container metrics like `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`.

**Why this hurts JVMs specifically.** GC briefly uses many threads. G1's parallel young GC scales to use all available cores during the pause. ZGC's concurrent threads run in the background. Both blow through CPU quota during these bursts and then get throttled. The result: a 10ms minor GC becomes a 60ms hiccup because the kernel paused the JVM mid-GC.

**Solutions, in order of preference:**

**1. Set CPU `requests` but no `limits`.** This is the recommended pattern in modern Kubernetes shops. The pod is guaranteed its requested CPU but can burst when needed. There is no throttling because there is no quota. The downside is potential noisy-neighbor effects on shared nodes — usually acceptable.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "2"        # guaranteed minimum
    memory: "2Gi"
  limits:
    memory: "2Gi"   # OOMKill on exceed
    # NO cpu limit - can burst freely
```

**2. Set CPU `limits` significantly higher than `requests`.** If you must use CPU limits (organizational policy, dedicated nodes), make the limit at least 2-3x the request to allow GC bursts.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: "2Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: "4"        # 4x burst headroom for GC
    memory: "2Gi"
```

**3. Override `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount`.** If cgroup CPU detection misbehaves (rare with modern Java but possible), you can force the JVM to size its thread pools for a specific count. This is a last resort.

```bash
-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2
```

**Diagnosing throttling.** Look for `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total` in Prometheus or the equivalent in your monitoring stack. Any non-zero value means throttling is occurring. Correlating throttling spikes with latency p99 spikes confirms the cause.

sections.title: Cold Starts — AppCDS, AOT, CRaC, and Native Image
sections.content:
Spring Boot 3 typically starts in 3-8 seconds. For long-lived pods, this is fine. For autoscaling, deploy frequency, or serverless environments, it is not. Three mechanisms reduce cold-start time without rewriting application code.

**Option 1: AppCDS (Application Class Data Sharing).** Pre-process the application's class metadata into a shared archive that the JVM memory-maps at startup. Cuts startup by 20-40%.

```dockerfile
# Multi-stage Dockerfile with AppCDS
FROM eclipse-temurin:21 AS appcds-builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY app.jar .
# Run once to record loaded classes
RUN java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=/build/app.jsa -jar app.jar --spring.context.exit=onRefresh || true

FROM eclipse-temurin:21
COPY --from=appcds-builder /build/app.jar /app/app.jar
COPY --from=appcds-builder /build/app.jsa /app/app.jsa
CMD ["java", "-XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

Rebuild the archive when dependencies change. CI integration makes this transparent.

**Option 2: Spring Boot AOT processing.** Spring Boot 3+ can generate bean definitions as source code at build time, eliminating the reflection-based classpath scanning that dominates Spring startup. Activate with `spring-boot-maven-plugin` AOT support.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <process-aot>true</process-aot>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

Combines well with AppCDS — AOT reduces the work, AppCDS skips the parsing.

**Option 3: CRaC (Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint).** A Java 17+ feature that snapshots a fully-warm running JVM (caches populated, JIT-compiled code, classes loaded) and restores it in under a second. Use Azul Zulu CRaC builds or AdoptOpenJDK with CRaC enabled.

```bash
# Take checkpoint after warming up
jcmd <pid> JDK.checkpoint

# Later, restore from checkpoint
java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=/path/to/checkpoint -jar app.jar
```

Trade-off: the checkpoint contains everything in memory at snapshot time, including secrets and connection state. Restore must invalidate stale connections.

**Option 4: GraalVM Native Image.** Compiles the entire application to a native binary at build time. Sub-100ms startup, lower memory footprint. Trade-offs: requires explicit reflection configuration, slower build (5-15 minutes), no JIT warmup so peak throughput may be lower than HotSpot, and not all libraries support it.

```bash
./mvnw -Pnative native:compile
./target/app   # starts in <100ms
```

**Choosing between them:**
- **AppCDS** — easy win for any Spring Boot app; always enable
- **AOT** — additional 20-30% startup improvement on Spring Boot 3+
- **CRaC** — when you need sub-second cold starts but want full HotSpot semantics
- **Native Image** — for serverless functions and minimal-footprint deployments where HotSpot's startup is unacceptable

sections.title: Production Kubernetes Deployment — Putting It All Together
sections.content:
A complete production-quality Kubernetes deployment for a Spring Boot service.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: order-service
        image: registry.example.com/order-service:1.4.2
        env:
        - name: JAVA_OPTS
          value: >-
            -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
            -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70
            -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=384m
            -XX:+UseG1GC
            -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
            -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
            -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
            -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/
            -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m
            -XX:StartFlightRecording=maxage=12h,maxsize=1g,filename=/var/recordings/app.jfr,dumponexit=true
            -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa
            -Dspring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "2Gi"
            cpu: "1"
          limits:
            memory: "2Gi"   # equal to request - no overcommit
            # NO cpu limit - allow GC bursting
        volumeMounts:
        - name: dumps
          mountPath: /dumps
        - name: recordings
          mountPath: /var/recordings
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /actuator/health/readiness
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /actuator/health/liveness
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
      volumes:
      - name: dumps
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: jvm-dumps
      - name: recordings
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: jvm-recordings
      - name: logs
        emptyDir: {}
```

Decisions encoded in this spec:
- **Memory request = limit** — no overcommit, predictable behavior
- **CPU request only** — allows GC to burst without throttling
- **70% MaxRAMPercentage** — leaves 600MB for non-heap on a 2GB container (room for Spring beans, Netty buffers, code cache)
- **G1GC with 200ms target** — appropriate for general web service workload
- **AppCDS archive** mounted from image — startup ~40% faster
- **Continuous JFR** to persistent volume — incident forensics available
- **Heap dumps to PVC** — survive pod restart on OOM
- **Virtual threads enabled** — Spring Boot 3.2+ I/O scaling
- **Separate readiness and liveness** — readiness fails immediately on issues; liveness gives more time to recover before pod restart

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three problems unique to containers** — cgroup resource detection, CPU quota throttling, cold start latency.
- **`-XX:+UseContainerSupport`** — default since Java 10; reads cgroup limits.
- **`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70-75`** — leaves room for non-heap (Metaspace, code cache, stacks, direct buffers).
- **Set `Initial == Max RAMPercentage`** — avoids heap-resize pauses.
- **CPU `requests` only, no `limits`** — prevents throttling during GC bursts; common modern pattern.
- **If CPU limits required** — set 2-3x the request for GC headroom.
- **AppCDS** — easy 20-40% startup improvement; always enable.
- **Spring Boot AOT + AppCDS** — combined, can cut Spring startup by 50%.
- **CRaC** — sub-second cold starts via running-JVM snapshot.
- **GraalVM native image** — sub-100ms startup; requires reflection config and compatibility testing.
- **Always**: GC logging, HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, persistent volume for dumps and recordings.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Tuning a JVM for microservices in containers is fundamentally different from tuning for bare-metal servers. Three things change.

**1. The JVM must read its resources from cgroups, not the host.**
- `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` is default since Java 10 — reads cgroup memory and CPU
- Use `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70-75` instead of hardcoded `-Xmx` — accounts for container memory limits
- Set `InitialRAMPercentage = MaxRAMPercentage` to avoid heap-resize pauses
- Reserve 25-30% for non-heap: Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers

**2. CPU quotas behave differently from CPU counts.**
- Pods with CPU limits get throttled during GC bursts — 10ms minor GC becomes 60ms hiccup
- **Modern pattern: CPU requests only, no limits** — pod is guaranteed minimum but can burst freely
- If CPU limits are required, set 2-3x the request for GC headroom
- Diagnose throttling via `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total` metrics

**3. Cold starts matter for autoscaling and deploys.**
- **AppCDS** — 20-40% startup improvement; always enable
- **Spring Boot AOT** — eliminates reflection scanning at runtime
- **CRaC** — restore a fully-warm JVM in under a second from a snapshot
- **GraalVM native image** — sub-100ms startup, but build complexity and reflection limitations

**Memory configuration discipline:**
- Set `requests = limits` for memory — no overcommit, predictable behavior
- Mount persistent volume for `/dumps` so OOM heap dumps survive pod restart
- Pair with `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` so OOM triggers a clean restart

**Garbage collector choice:**
- **G1** for general web services, default since Java 9
- **ZGC** when p99 latency requirements are stricter than G1's 200ms target
- **Parallel GC** for batch jobs that prioritize throughput

**Observability essentials in production:**
- Continuous **GC logging** with `-Xlog:gc*`
- Continuous **JFR** for incident forensics
- **HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError** to a persistent volume
- Separate **readiness** and **liveness** probes

In an interview, the differentiator is mentioning the CPU throttling trap — most candidates know about MaxRAMPercentage, far fewer understand why CPU limits hurt JVMs specifically.
